title: Up the hill, weeping (2 Samuel 15:30)
hook: the fleeing king climbs the Mount of Olives barefoot, head covered

segments.voice: Yesterday, Absalom at the gate, telling everyone they were right. Your line was he stole their hearts. Did you notice any flattery? Today, those stolen hearts turn into a revolt, and his father leaves the city on foot. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

A messenger runs into the palace with one sentence: the hearts of the men of Israel are after Absalom. Absalom has had himself proclaimed king in Hebron, and he's coming. David doesn't try to hold the city. He says: arise, let us flee, or none of us will escape him. And so the king of Israel walks out of his own city, his household behind him, crosses the brook Kidron, and starts up the slope on the far side. Not riding. Walking. Barefoot.
screen: `THE HEARTS ARE AFTER ABSALOM.` → `ARISE, LET US FLEE.` → `ACROSS THE KIDRON, ON FOOT.`

segments.voice: The verse is a slow picture. David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, and "wept as he went up". His head was covered. He went barefoot. And all the people with him covered their heads too, and they went up weeping as they went. Covered head and bare feet: some readers see a mourner in them. A king who once danced before the ark with all his might now climbs a hill like a mourner. In Hebrew the verse keeps saying the same two things: going up, weeping. Up and weeping, up and weeping, one step at a time. What's striking is what David does on the way. He doesn't give up. He sends the priests back to the city with the ark: if I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, he says, God will bring me back and let me see it again. And if not, here I am; let God do to me what seems good. Then he hears that Ahithophel, his own wise counselor, has joined Absalom, and he prays a short, practical prayer: turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness. And at the very top, where God was worshipped, a loyal friend named Hushai is waiting for him with his coat torn and earth on his head. David gives him a job. So the climb is two things at once. It is grief, honest and out loud, in front of everyone. And it is still movement. Weeping didn't stop David from walking, and walking didn't stop him weeping. He let the hard day be hard, and he kept going up the hill.
screen: `HEAD COVERED. BAREFOOT.` · then, large: `UP THE HILL, WEEPING.` · then: `IF I FIND FAVOR, HE WILL BRING ME BACK.` · `A FRIEND WAITS AT THE TOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk humbly through a hard day. Settle, and breathe. If your feet are free, press them flat on the floor and feel the ground, the way a barefoot walker would. Bring to mind something heavy you're carrying right now, or one you carried not long ago. You don't need to fix it or pretend it's light. Just name it, and then name the next small step: one email, one call, one meal. Weeping and walking can happen together. If you pray, you can say David's words: here I am. The bell holds the time.
Up the hill. David leaving Jerusalem, climbing the Mount of Olives barefoot, head covered, still moving. Today's word.
Your line: up the hill, weeping. Today, if the day is hard, let it be hard, and take the next step anyway. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Jews read David's flight from Jerusalem as part of the book of Samuel; the heading of Psalm 3 links that psalm to the time David fled from Absalom his son.

original.note: Hebrew: going up and weeping, from 2 Samuel 15:30.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king running away.
what it means: David grieves openly, head covered and barefoot, and still keeps moving and planning.
what a scholar hears: the verse repeats going up and weeping, first for David, then for all the people with him.

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording 'wept as he went up' at 2 Samuel 15:30.
Hebrew in 'original' (עֹלֶה וּבוֹכֶה) should be checked against the Masoretic text of 15:30.
'Covered head and bare feet are signs of mourning elsewhere' (e.g. Esther 6:12, Ezekiel 24:17) is stated generally; Keeper may wish to cite.
The back-reference to 'with all his might' is day 744 (2 Samuel 6:14).
David's words to Zadok (15:25–26), his prayer about Ahithophel (15:31) and Hushai at the summit (15:32) are paraphrased.
Psalm 3's heading is mentioned only in howItsDone.
Editor pass: softened the general mourning-sign claim to 'some readers'; 'where people used to bow down' changed to the text's 'where God was worshipped' (15:32).
Audit: garbled review line ('the hearts he stole come due') rewritten; 'doesn't call for a siege' (David was the one who would be besieged) changed to 'doesn't try to hold the city' (15:14).
